You're designing a part for someone to 3D print at home. They'll print it on their own printer, use only the hardware listed below, and put it together by following your manual.

## Their setup
- Printer: Bambu Lab X1C (with AMS), build volume 256 x 256 x 256 mm
- Nozzle: 0.4 mm
- Layer height: 0.2 mm
- Filament: PLA (high-speed PLA, black)
- Longest bridge seen to print cleanly on this setup: 50 mm
- Supports: none. Every part has to print without them.

## Hardware they can use
Refer to an item by its catalog reference: "ISO 4762 M5x30" (socket head screw, size x length, from the lengths listed), "ISO 4032 M5" (hex nut), "ISO 10511 M5" (nylon-insert lock nut), "ISO 7089 M5" (washer), "ASME B18.2.2 1/4-20" (1/4"-20 nut), "insert M3x4x5" (heat-set insert), "salvaged:webcam-mount-bolt".

```yaml

  M3: 0.5
  M4: 0.7
  M5: 0.8
  M6: 1.0
  M8: 1.25
  1/4-20: 1.27
screws:
- family: socket head cap screw
  standard: ISO 4762
  head: cylindrical
  sizes:
    M3:
      d: 3
      head_d: 5.5
      head_h: 3
      b: 18
      threaded_to_head_max: 20
    M4:
      d: 4
      head_d: 7.0
      head_h: 4
      b: 20
      threaded_to_head_max: 25
    M5:
      d: 5
      head_d: 8.5
      head_h: 5
      b: 22
      threaded_to_head_max: 25
    M6:
      d: 6
      head_d: 10.0
      head_h: 6
      b: 24
      threaded_to_head_max: 30
    M8:
      d: 8
      head_d: 13.0
      head_h: 8
      b: 28
      threaded_to_head_max: 35
  lengths_mm:
  - 6
  - 8
  - 10
  - 12
  - 16
  - 20
  - 25
  - 30
  - 35
  - 40
  - 45
  - 50
nuts:
- family: hex nut
  standard: ISO 4032
  sizes:
    M3:
      af: 5.5
      h: 2.4
    M4:
      af: 7.0
      h: 3.2
    M5:
      af: 8.0

  standard: ISO 10511
  sizes:

      af: 5.5

    M4:

    M5:

    M6:
      af: 10.0
      h: 6.0
    M8:
      af: 13.0
      h: 8.0
- family: hex nut
  standard: ASME B18.2.2 (finished hex)
  sizes:
    1/4-20:
      af: 11.11
      h: 5.56
      af_measured: 10.92

  standard: ISO 7089
  sizes:
    M3:
      id: 3.2
      od: 7
      t: 0.5
    M4:
      id: 4.3
      od: 9
      t: 0.8
    M5:
      id: 5.3

      t: 1.0

      id: 6.4
      od: 12
      t: 1.6
    M8:
      id: 8.4
      od: 16
      t: 1.6
inserts:
- family: heat-set threaded insert
  standard: none (vendor-specific)
  sizes:
    M3x4x5:
      thread: M3
      length: 4
      od: 5
      hole_d: 4.3
salvaged:
- id: webcam-mount-bolt
  description: 1/4"-20 bolt from a webcam monitor mount
  thread: 1/4-20
  head_d: null
  head_h: null
  length: null
servos:
- id: MG90S
  body_l:
    measured:
    - 22.0
    - 22.63
    note: two readings of the length; 22.63 used
  body_w:
    measured: 12.33
  body_h:
    measured: 22.5
    note: '''top to bottom''; not used by the coupon'
  spline_od:
    measured: 4.57
  tab_hole_d:
    measured: 2.17
  tab_top_to_case_top:
    measured: 1.67
    note: from the tab's top face (same method as MG996R)
  tab_t:
    measured: 2.55
  tab_face_to_case_top:
    used: 4.22
    note: tab top to case top + tab thickness (1.67 + 2.55)
  tab_hole_pitch:
    measured: 25.84
    used: 28.01
    note: caliper tips closed into the two holes, so inner edges; centres = 25.84
      + 2.17. Datasheet ~27.8
- id: MG996R
  body_l:
    measured: 40.58
  body_w:
    measured: 19.82
  body_h:
    measured:
    - 40.41
    - 40.4
    note: '''front to back'''
  output_top_d:
    measured: 5.6
    note: '''the thing at the top''; unclear which feature'
  spline_od:
    measured: 5.84
    note: '''if I grab here'''
  tab_hole_d:
    measured: 4.58
  tab_hole_pitch:
    measured: 44.61
    used: 49.19
    note: inner edges as for MG90S; centres = 44.61 + 4.58. Datasheet ~49.5. Spacing
      across each tab's hole pair not measured (datasheet 10)
  tab_shape:
    note: each tab has two holes open to the edge (U-slots) and a stiffening rib on
      its top face (the shaft side) between them; the cable leaves the case end below
      the tabs (photos IMG_5454-5456, indexed in docs/media/photos.md)
  mounting:
    note: seated from below (shaft up through the plate), the tab's top face meets
      the plate, so the rib must be relieved and the case rises tab_top_to_case_top
      above the plate; seated from above, the tab's underside meets it and the case
      rises tab_face_to_case_top
  horns_in_box:
    note: plastic double-arm, 6-arm star, round disc, 4-arm cross; plus a bought 25T
      aluminium single arm with a clamped split hub and 2 holes (IMG_5457-5458). aluminium
      arm measured below (horn_25t_aluminium); plastic horns unmeasured
  tab_notch:
    width:
      measured: 1.51
    protrudes:
      measured: 1.8
      note: Dan confirmed 1.8 mm
    from_hole_side:
      measured: 8.31
      note: '''from the side of the holes to the middle notch'''
    note: a feature between each tab's two holes that stops the tabs sitting flush
      (coupon D, round 2)
  tab_t:
    measured: 2.28
  tab_top_to_case_top:
    measured:
    - 5.63
    - 5.69
    used: 5.69
    note: 'Dan, with a sketch: from the tab''s top face'
  tab_face_to_case_top:
    used: 7.97
    note: tab top to case top + tab thickness (5.69 + 2.28); the tab's underside sits
      on the mount
  horn_25t_aluminium:
    hub_od:
      measured: 14.66
    overall_l:
      measured: 34.62
      note: hub's far edge to arm tip
    hub_t:
      measured: 5.95
    arm_t:
      measured: 3.86
    end_boss_t:
      measured: 5.95
      note: '''on the foot, there''s a stickout'': the raised end around the holes'
    centre_to_tip:
      used: 27.29
      note: overall_l - hub_od / 2
    hole_centres_from_hub:
      estimated:
      - 20.4
      - 24.1
      note: from photo IMG_5457 proportions scaled to centre_to_tip; about +-1 mm,
        not measured
    hole_d:
      measured: 2.55
      note: from the earlier readings ('these little holes')
    earlier_readings:
      note: 3.13 (likely the clamp screw hole), 1.52, 4.43, 65.88 (heard as '6.5.88');
        features unconfirmed
bearings:
- id: 608ZZ
  od:
    measured: 21.22
    used: 22.0
    note: 608 OD is 22.000 -0.008; the video shows the bearing pinched at the jaw
      tips at an angle, which reads low. Re-measure
  bore:
    measured: 7.94
    nominal: 8.0
  width:
    measured: null
    nominal: 7.0
```

## How to work
You have these tools:
- measure(item, what): ask the person to measure one of their own things, such as their desk or their phone. They answer with what they measured, or say they can't measure it.
- print_test(params, parts): optional. If you need to know whether something is going to work but you're not sure, ask the person to print a test of it before you hand in the final design, so you both save time and filament. They print it and tell you how each piece came out.
- submit_design(...): hand in the finished design. This ends the conversation.
- report_limitation(wanted, blocked_by, why): say you wanted to use something (a technique, a tool, a part or material, a way of handing in the design) but couldn't because of what's available here. It doesn't change anything, but it's noted.
You have at most 12 turns. Hand in a design before they run out.

## The design you hand in
submit_design's schema describes every field. The rules that matter:
- Every dimension that comes from hardware or the real world is a named param, with its source: measured (the person measured it for you), datasheet, catalog, asked (the person told you), guessed, unknown, or design (your own choice).
- Each part's `code` is Python that defines build(p) and returns a CadQuery Workplane or Shape. `cq` is already imported, and p.<name> is each param's value. Dimensions that come from hardware or the real world must come from params.
- Model each part in the orientation it's printed in, with z = 0 on the bed.
- The manual is the steps the person follows, naming the parts and hardware each step uses.

The roller wheel on my sliding closet door snapped. I've got two 608 skateboard bearings and an M8 bolt I could use. Could I 3D print a new wheel that spins on the bolt? The old one was about 50 mm across and about 16 mm wide.

reasoning:
We need to design a replacement roller wheel for a sliding closet door, that spins on... wait, they mention two 608 bearings and an M8 bolt. The 608 bearing has 8mm bore — so it could ride directly on the M8 bolt (M8 is 8mm shaft but threaded... M8 bolt shaft is ~7.8-7.9 mm, thread crest 8.0). Hmm, 608 bore is 8.0 nominal. An M8 bolt shaft OD is about 7.9mm (for a rolled thread, major diameter is a bit less than 8.0). Actually M8 external thread major diameter max is 8.0 -0.02ish. So 7.9ish, and bore 8.0 +0.008/-0. Nominal 8.000 -0.008. So the bolt would fit with ~0.1mm clearance. But the bolt is threaded all along the shank portion, and it's not a smooth shaft. Better: use the bearing as the rolling element and the bolt as axle.

Let me think about the design. The key insight: the 608 bearing OD is 22mm, which is much smaller than the 50mm wheel. So the printed wheel must be a tire/tyre that presses onto the 608 bearing OD. Two 608 bearings, stacked, would give a 14mm wide bearing assembly — close to the 16mm wide wheel. Actually 2 × 7 = 14mm. So the wheel outer part (tyre) is printed with a bore that press-fits onto the 608 OD (22mm), and it's 16mm wide, with the two bearings press-fit inside, and an M8 bolt through the 8mm bores as the axle.

Bearing OD 22.000 -0.008 nominal. Measured 21.22 which is unreliable (the notes say pinched at jaw tips giving a low reading). We should use the datasheet 22.0.

Need a press fit for 22mm into PLA. FDM printing of a 22mm bore — typical practice: make the bore slightly undersized, e.g. 21.7-21.8 for a press fit, or slightly oversized for a slip. Since we can't ream it, a press fit into a printed hole with horizontal holes can be tricky. Alternative: print the wheel in two halves that clamp around the bearings? Or print the wheel with a 22.6 bore and glue the bearings in (CA glue). Gluing is fine but the manual should mention. Actually simpler: press fit with a slight interference. But FDM holes typically print undersized, so a nominal 22.0 bore would be tight. Hmm.

Better approach: print a test coupon to determine the right bore size for a snug/press fit of the 608. Use print_test with a coupon that has several bores (21.6, 21.8, 22.0, 22.2, 22.4) so the person tells which fits the bearing best. That's a good use of the coupon tool. But we only have 12 turns. We can do maybe 1-2 coupons.

Also the outer diameter: 50mm across as the old one. Wheel width 16mm.

Wait — how does the wheel attach to the sliding door? The old wheel presumably had a bracket/axle attached to the door. The user says "the roller wheel snapped" and wants a new wheel that spins on the M8 bolt. They have the bolt. The bolt presumably goes through the door's bracket/hanger. Hmm, we don't know the door mounting. We should ask them to measure the door hardware: the axle hole in the bracket / the original axle diameter, the wheel O.D., wheel width. They already gave 50mm across, 16mm wide.

Also: is the M8 bolt long enough? They didn't say length. We need a param for that — guessed or asked. Hmm, we can't ask (measure tool is for measuring their things — actually measure can be used: "ask the person to measure one of their own things" — the M8 bolt is one of their things! Yes, we can use measure on the bolt: length, and the shank diameter).

Let me use measure tool calls:
1. Measure the old broken wheel's... it snapped; maybe they still have pieces. Measure the old wheel: outer diameter, width, and the bore/hub where the axle passed. Actually the key is the axle diameter in the original wheel.
2. Measure the M8 bolt: total length under head, and the shank/unthreaded length — important for press fit consideration.
3. Measure the door's hanger/bracket: hole center height? Hmm.

Actually, let's think about what really matters:

The wheel: OD 50, width 16, bore for two 608 bearings (22 OD, 8 bore), axle M8 bolt through the bearings. The bolt must be long enough to pass through both bearings (14mm) plus whatever mounts to the door (bracket) plus a nut. If the bolt is short, we may need to use one bearing only.

Hmm, an important subtlety: if the bolt passes through the printed wheel's bore... wait, no. If the bearings are press-fit in the wheel, the bolt goes through the bearing bores (8mm), and the wheel spins on the bearings around the bolt. The bolt is clamped to the door bracket, stationary. That's the standard design. Good. So the axle diameter in the printed part is the bearing OD (22), not 8.

So the printed wheel is: a 50mm OD, 16mm wide tyre with a central through-bore of 22mm (bearing seat) — with a shoulder/stop so the bearings sit at the right depth, and maybe a small lip to retain them.

Design details:
- Tyre: outer OD 50, width 16.
- Central bore 22mm x 16mm deep, but we want a ridge in the middle to locate the two bearings? No — the two bearings stack: 7+7 = 14mm, leaving 2mm. If we put them flush at each face, there'd be a 2mm gap in the middle, fine. Actually wait: the bearings need a shoulder to press against so they don't go in too far. If the bore is a through hole 22mm and we press the bearing from each side until flush, they'd sit at 0-7 and 9-16 → 2mm gap in the middle at 7-9. That's fine — the bolt passes through both. But the bolt is M8: the bearings' 8mm bore. The bolt threads pass through the smooth bearing bore — fine, it's a light fit.

Hmm, but wait: should the bolt actually be the axle, with the wheel spinning on the bearings? Yes. But actually if the bolt is clamped tight against the two bearing inner rings, the wheel spins freely on the bearings. That's the classic skate wheel arrangement.

Alternatively, they could just put the bolt through the plain printed hole — but bolt threads would chew the plastic. Bearings are better. Use both bearings.

Key fit parameters:
- Bearing OD: 22.0 (datasheet), hole diameter in the print: press fit. Typical FDM: print a hole 0.1-0.2 undersize... actually for a press fit you want interference. But FDM holes shrink/print undersized already. To be safe, use a coupon.

Let me plan the coupon: a small test piece, printed in the same orientation as the final wheel (axis vertical? or horizontal?). Important: the bore axis orientation matters for print accuracy. If the wheel is printed flat (axis vertical, i.e., the wheel lying on the bed like a disc), then the 22mm bore is a circular hole in a horizontal plane → prints accurate-ish, but the wheel would need to be 50mm wide... no. Wait.

Wheel: 50mm diameter, 16mm thick along the axle. Printed in what orientation?
Option A: lying flat — the 50mm disc face on the bed, z from 0 to 16. Then the bore is a vertical hole (axis Z). Circular holes with vertical axis print with good roundness; the OD is a circle in XY → good. Layer lines run across the wheel face; the rolling surface is the cylindrical side wall, printed as stacked outlines — good for rolling. This is the best orientation: the wheel's outer surface is the print's side walls... wait no. If the wheel lies flat (disc on the bed), the cylindrical outer surface (the tread) is the vertical wall of the cylinder — printed as vertical walls, which are strong and smooth. The bearing bore is a vertical circular hole. Great. And no supports needed. Height 16mm, diameter 50mm — fine.

Option B: on its side (like a wheel standing) — needs supports for the bore and is weak. No.

So Option A. Print orientation: disc face on bed, z = 0 to 16.

Coupon: to test the 22mm bearing bore fit, print a test disc with several bores. Since the fit is an interference/slip fit for the bearing, a coupon with bores at 21.6, 21.8, 22.0, 22.2 would tell us which gives a snug press fit. Also test the M8 clearance? The M8 bolt goes through the bearing bore, not the printed part. But it might also need to pass through a printed flange? Hmm — do we need a printed part on the door side? The user only asked for a wheel. But how does the bolt attach to the door? Presumably the original hanger bracket has a slot/hole that the old axle went through. Reusing the M8 bolt: the bolt head on one side, and a nut on the other side of the bracket. But the bracket hole may be smaller than 8mm.

Hmm, this is a real question. We should ask the user to measure the door bracket: the hole/slot width where the axle passes. Actually more robust: design the wheel so that it also works if the bolt goes through a hanger bracket of some thickness. But we don't know the bracket. Let's ask them to measure:
- The old wheel: hub bore diameter (the axle hole in the broken wheel pieces) — tells us the original axle size.
- The door's hanger bracket: the opening where the axle passes (width and the material thickness).
- The M8 bolt: shank length under the head, and the unthreaded portion length, plus the head diameter/height.

That's a lot of measurements. The measure tool takes one item/dimension at a time. We have 12 turns. Let's be economical: maybe 3-4 measure calls in parallel (they're independent, so batch them in one block).

Actually the instructions say to batch independent calls in one block. Let's do:

Turn 1: measure calls:
1. measure("the M8 bolt", "length of the shank from under the head to the tip")
2. measure("the M8 bolt", "diameter of the smooth shank (not the threads) if it has any, else just the bolt")
3. measure("the sliding door's hanger bracket", "the diameter or slot width of the hole the old wheel's axle went through, and the bracket thickness")
4. measure("the broken wheel pieces", "the diameter of the centre hole the axle passed through")

Hmm, but the person may not be able to measure all. Let's do it anyway; they can say they can't.

Actually careful: I should keep it focused. The most critical unknowns:
(a) Is the M8 bolt long enough? Needs ≥ 16 (wheel) + bracket thickness + nut. Ask length.
(b) Bore fit for the 608 in PLA — solved by coupon.
(c) How the wheel mounts to the door — need the bracket's axle hole size and the bracket thickness, plus whether the wheel sits in a channel/track with clearance (the wheel OD 50 is given).

Also, the door: sliding closet doors ride in a top track or bottom track. The wheel OD matters for riding in the track. They said ~50mm across and ~16mm wide — we'll use those.

Another consideration: the M8 bolt's threaded portion passing through the 608 bearing bore. A rolled M8 thread has major diameter ~7.87-8.0; bearing bore 8.0 +0/-0.008. So it should be a slip fit; a die-cut thread might be exactly 8.0 and too tight. It's usually fine. But if the bolt is threaded where the bearing sits, the bearing's inner ring sits on the thread crests. Fine, it's a roller.

Also should we include a washer / spacer between the bolt head and the bearing, or between the bracket and bearing? ISO 7089 M8 washers are in the list. Using two M8 washers: one under the head, one under the nut, so the clamping force goes to the bearing inner rings and not bind. And a nylon-insert lock nut ISO 10511 M8 to keep it from loosening. M8 locknut: af 13, h 8. The bolt must be long enough: 16 (wheel) + 2×1.6 (washers, both sides... actually one inside the wheel? no) — let's count: bolt head → washer → (bearing inner ring) → bracket → washer → locknut. Hmm wait, where's the bracket? Let's think: the wheel hangs on the bolt; the bolt is fixed to the hanger bracket. Typical: bracket has a hole; the bolt goes through the bracket and through the wheel's bearings, with a nut. Order along the bolt: [bolt head] [bracket] ... [wheel] [nut]? or [bolt head] [wheel] [bracket] [nut]? Depends. Simplest generic: bolt head — washer — wheel (bearings) — bracket — washer — lock nut. Hmm, but then the wheel is between the head and the bracket: force path: head → bearing inner ring (left) → bearing inner ring (right) → bracket → nut. Yes, the bearings' inner rings are clamped, wheel spins. Good.

But we don't know the bracket thickness. Ask.

Hmm — do we actually need to know the bracket? The user is replacing just the wheel. They'll reuse the existing bracket and presumably a bolt that fits it. If the original axle was smaller than M8 (e.g., 5/16" or 6mm), the M8 bolt may not fit their bracket hole. That's why I ask for the bracket hole.

Hmm, but the design I hand in is a wheel. The "world" hardware is the door bracket. I could design the wheel's bore to accept the 608 bearings regardless. The mounting is up to the reused bolt. But I should still verify the bolt length and bracket hole to give a good manual.

Let's think about the second 608 bearing. Two bearings stacked in a 16mm-wide wheel with a 22mm bore: 14mm of bearing + 2mm gap. If instead we want the bearings flush at the outer faces and the middle gap 2mm, the bolt must bridge the 2mm gap — fine, the bolt is rigid.

Wait, but actually: is it better to just have the bearings' inner rings not clamped and instead let the whole assembly be clamped? If both bearings' inner rings are clamped by the head and nut, the outer rings rotate with the tyre. Excellent.

Also, we should add a "flange/lip" in the printed wheel to keep the bearings from being pushed all the way through — but if the bore is a through hole at 22.0 and we press from both sides, each bearing stops when flush with the face only if there's a shoulder. Without a shoulder, you could press a bearing in too deep. So add a small internal rib: e.g., at mid-depth, a ring of 24mm ID × 2mm... hmm, the middle 2mm region could be a smaller diameter (say 23.5mm, no wait, it must clear nothing... Actually it just needs to be smaller than 22 so the bearing can't pass). Let's make the central 2mm-wide band with a bore of 20mm (a shelf). Then each bearing seats against this shelf → they'd be at 0-7 and 9-16 with a 2mm internal groove of 20mm diameter. But then the two 8mm bores are aligned and the bolt passes through the 20mm groove region — fine. Wait, the bolt through the 20mm region: fine, no contact.

Hmm, but actually a 20mm-diameter internal groove band: the print would have a 20mm hole from 7 to 9 — that's an internal overhang? No — it's a hole: the wall at 22mm from z=0-7, then a step to 20mm from 7-9, then 22mm from 9-16. The step at z=7 is an "overhang" — a horizontal annular face facing down (a ceiling) of width 1mm ((22-20)/2). That's a 1mm-wide horizontal overhang at 7mm height — printable without support? It's a bridge-like feature but only 1mm wide annular ring; in a circular hole, the layer at z=7 prints a circle at 22mm then steps in to 20mm; the unsupported overhang is only 1mm (the annulus between r=10 and r=11) — that's fine for a 0.4 nozzle (2.5 line widths) and 1mm bridges fine (max bridge is 50mm).

Alternatively, make the shoulder a taper/chamfer. Simplest: give each bearing seat a shelf: bore 22.0 for 7.5mm from each face, and the middle 1mm a shelf at 20mm. Hmm.

Or simpler geometry: make the through-bore 22.0mm for the whole 16mm, and press the bearings flush. A through bore with no shoulder can't locate precisely, but honestly, press the first bearing in until its inner face is 8mm... You can't easily control. Use a shoulder: it's cheap. I'll go with a middle shelf.

Actually here's a cleaner approach: give the bore three zones:
- z 0–7: 22.0 (bearing seat, press fit)
- z 7–9: 20.0 (shelf, but that shelf creates a downward ceiling at z=7 — 1mm ring)
- z 9–16: 22.0

Hmm wait: but for a printed part, having an internal ledge like this means the through-hole is printed from the bottom layer: layers 0-7 at r=11, layer 7-9 at r=10, 9-16 at r=11. The transition at z=7 from r=11 to r=10 is a step out (the material grows inward) — no overhang problem at all! Growing inward = the new layer at z=7.2 is a ring from r=10 to r=11 resting entirely on the previous layer. Yes! That's fine, it's an inward step, fully supported. The other transition at z=9 from r=10 to r=11 (hole widening) — that's a downward-facing ceiling of 1mm width, an overhang. 1mm cantilever, fine (45° rule: 1mm out over 0.2mm layer = 78° — not great, but it's only 1mm wide and unsupported 1mm is nothing; also many slicers handle it. Actually a 1mm-wide horizontal ceiling ring means the layer at z=9 prints over air for 1mm width. That's a small bridge — 1mm bridge is trivially fine).

Alternatively, make the shelf a cone/chamfer. Let's keep it simple: shelf with a 45° chamfer maybe. Eh, 1mm flat is fine. Actually let's reconsider — maybe better: make each bearing seat have a chamfered lead-in at each face (helps pressing in) and a mid shelf.

Let me simplify further: mid shelf 2mm wide, diameter 20.

But hold on. Do we even want a press fit? Press fit in PLA with 0.4mm nozzle: a 22mm bore printed will come out maybe 21.8-21.9. To be safe, print a coupon with bore sizes and let the user pick. But the final part's bore must be a single value from params. I'll use a param `bearing_seat_d` with source "coupon"? The allowed sources: measured, datasheet, catalog, asked, guessed, unknown, design. Hmm, no "coupon" source. I'd set it to "design" with a note that the coupon confirmed it. Or "measured" if they measure the printed bore. Let's just do the coupon to pick the value, then declare it as design/measured.

Plan the coupon: a small test plate (a few mm thick, e.g. 6mm) with bores: 21.5, 21.7, 21.9, 22.1, 22.3. The user presses the 608 into each and reports which is snug-but-pressable. Then we use that value. That's a good use of print_test. But 5 bores vs. print time — small.

Hmm, but there's another consideration: the fit should probably NOT be a press fit that requires force, because pressing a steel bearing into PLA can crack it, and also because press-fitting can distort. A common approach: print bore slightly larger and glue the bearing in with CA glue, or design a "capture" with a retaining ring. But simplest and robust: light press fit (0.1-0.2 interference) or a snug slip fit + a couple of dabs of CA glue. Let me let the coupon decide: the user can report which is snug and which needs glue.
